title: What other techniques help with data skew — isolate hot keys and broadcast them separately, increase parallelism, pre-aggregate before join, use a different join strategy, or redesign the data model?
shortTitle: Other techniques that help with data skew

s1_definition.profdef: Beyond salting and Adaptive Query Execution, data skew in Spark can be addressed by isolating the few hot keys and joining them with a broadcast while the cold keys go through a normal join, by increasing shuffle parallelism so the hot partition is at least split further, by pre-aggregating on the map side before the shuffle so far less data lands on the hot key, by switching to a join strategy that avoids shuffling the large side such as a broadcast hash join, or by redesigning the data model so the hot key no longer exists, for example by pre-splitting a pooling account into sub-accounts. Each technique attacks the imbalance from a different angle, and in production you usually combine two or three.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India one giant pooling account overwhelms a single clerk. You can pull that one account aside and handle it specially (isolate and broadcast), hire more clerks so the pile is cut into more sub-piles (increase parallelism), have each branch total its own slips before sending them in so the central clerk receives summaries instead of raw slips (pre-aggregate), route the work so the clerk never has to wait on the big ledger (different join strategy), or restructure the books so the one giant account becomes many smaller numbered sub-accounts (redesign the data model).
s1_definition.oneliner: Fight skew by isolating-and-broadcasting hot keys, increasing parallelism, pre-aggregating before the shuffle, changing the join strategy, or redesigning the model so the hot key disappears.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Beyond salting and Adaptive Query Execution, data skew in Spark can be addressed by isolating the few hot keys and joining them with a broadcast while the cold keys go through a normal join, by increasing shuffle parallelism so the hot partition is at least split further, by pre-aggregating on the map side before the shuffle so far less data lands on the hot key, by switching to a join strategy that avoids shuffling the large side such as a broadcast hash join, or by redesigning the data model so the hot key no longer exists, for example by pre-splitting a pooling account into sub-accounts. Each technique attacks the imbalance from a different angle, and in production you usually combine two or three.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India one giant pooling account overwhelms a single clerk. You can pull that one account aside and handle it specially (isolate and broadcast), hire more clerks so the pile is cut into more sub-piles (increase parallelism), have each branch total its own slips before sending them in so the central clerk receives summaries instead of raw slips (pre-aggregate), route the work so the clerk never has to wait on the big ledger (different join strategy), or restructure the books so the one giant account becomes many smaller numbered sub-accounts (redesign the data model).

**One line to remember:** Fight skew by isolating-and-broadcasting hot keys, increasing parallelism, pre-aggregating before the shuffle, changing the join strategy, or redesigning the model so the hot key disappears.

sections.s2_technical:
Isolate-and-broadcast is the most surgical technique when the hot keys are few and known. You split the join into two branches. First you filter the large table to just the hot keys and join that slice with a broadcast of the matching small-side rows, which are tiny for a handful of keys, so no shuffle of the huge hot partition happens. Then you filter to the cold keys and run a normal shuffle join. Finally you union the two results. In PySpark this is `big.filter(col("key").isin(hot)).join(broadcast(small_hot), "key")` unioned with `big.filter(~col("key").isin(hot)).join(small, "key")`. This removes the hot key from the shuffle path entirely.

Increasing parallelism means raising `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` so the hashing spreads keys across more partitions. This helps when many moderately-hot keys collide into the same partition, because more partitions reduce collisions. It does not help a single mega-key, because one key always hashes to exactly one partition regardless of partition count — that is why salting or isolate-and-broadcast is needed for a true single hot key.

Pre-aggregation before the join or at the map side dramatically reduces the data volume on the hot key. If you are joining transactions to accounts only to count per account, do the count first with `reduceByKey` or a `groupBy().agg()` that benefits from map-side combine, so each partition sends one partial count per key instead of millions of rows. Less data on the hot key means a smaller skewed partition. The general rule is to shrink the data before it crosses the shuffle boundary.

Choosing a different join strategy can sidestep skew. If the small side fits in memory, a broadcast hash join avoids shuffling the large skewed side at all, so no partition becomes a straggler. Conversely, forcing a sort-merge join when a broadcast would have worked can reintroduce skew. The strategy choice interacts with skew because only shuffle-based joins expose skew.

Redesigning the data model is the deepest fix. If a single pooling or suspense account is structurally hot, you can split it into several sub-accounts at the source so no single key dominates, or you can pre-compute the heavy aggregate in a separate batch so the hot join never runs online. A senior nuance is that model redesign is the most durable fix but the most expensive to implement, so you reach for it when the same hot key keeps causing incidents across many jobs rather than patching each job.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India a transactions table skews on a single corporate pooling account. The few hot keys are known, so isolating them and broadcasting their small-side account rows, then unioning with the cold-key join, removes the skew surgically.

Problem 2 — A different job has dozens of moderately-hot merchant keys colliding into the same shuffle partitions. Simply increasing shuffle parallelism spreads them out.

Problem 3 — A reporting job joins raw transactions to accounts only to produce per-account counts. Pre-aggregating the counts before the join shrinks the hot key's data so no partition is oversized.

The demo takes a skew situation described by how many hot keys there are, whether the keys are known, and whether the downstream only needs an aggregate, and recommends isolate-and-broadcast, increase-parallelism, or pre-aggregate, logging the reasoning so a junior engineer can follow it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three skew situations — a pooling-account join with one known hot key, a merchant job with forty unknown colliding keys, and a per-account count job that only needs an aggregate.

Step 1: The first situation enters `recommend`. It does not only need an aggregate, its one hot key is known and few, so the advisor returns isolate-and-broadcast. The data for this situation is the profile object; nothing is mutated, a string recommendation is produced.

Step 2: The second situation enters. It does not only need an aggregate, and its forty hot keys are not known, so the first two branches are skipped and the advisor returns increase-parallelism. The reasoning is logged.

Step 3: The third situation enters. It only needs an aggregate, so the very first branch fires and returns pre-aggregate before the join, which shrinks the hot key's data below the shuffle boundary.

Step 4: The demo logs each scenario with its chosen technique, giving a junior engineer a clear mapping from symptom to fix.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 05:00:01 INFO    Scenario txn-join-pooling-account → ISOLATE-AND-BROADCAST — remove the hot key from the shuffle path
2026-10-30 05:00:01 INFO    merchant-collisions: increase shuffle parallelism to spread colliding keys
2026-10-30 05:00:01 INFO    Scenario merchant-collisions → INCREASE-PARALLELISM — more shuffle partitions reduce key collisions
2026-10-30 05:00:01 INFO    per-account-counts: pre-aggregate before join (map-side combine)
2026-10-30 05:00:01 INFO    Scenario per-account-counts → PRE-AGGREGATE — reduce data on the hot key before the shuffle
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Beyond salting and Adaptive Query Execution, I keep a toolbox of skew techniques and pick based on the symptom. When there are a few known hot keys, I isolate and broadcast them: I filter those keys out of the large table, join them against a broadcast of their tiny small-side rows, run a normal shuffle join on the remaining cold keys, and union the two results, which removes the hot key from the shuffle path entirely. When many moderately-hot keys are colliding into the same partitions, I increase shuffle parallelism so the hashing spreads them out, though I am careful to note that raising partition count never helps a single true mega-key because one key always hashes to one partition.

When the downstream only needs an aggregate, I pre-aggregate before the shuffle so map-side combine sends one partial result per key instead of millions of raw rows, which shrinks the hot partition at the source. I also consider the join strategy itself, because only shuffle-based joins expose skew, so switching to a broadcast hash join when the small side fits in memory sidesteps the problem. The deepest fix is redesigning the data model, for example splitting a structurally hot pooling account into numbered sub-accounts so no single key dominates.

At the National Bank of India these were real decisions. A transactions join skewed on one corporate pooling account was cleanest with isolate-and-broadcast. A merchant job with dozens of colliding keys was fixed just by raising shuffle partitions. A per-account counting job was fixed by pre-aggregating before the join. My rule in interviews is to start with the cheapest and most surgical technique that fits the symptom, combine two or three when needed, and reserve model redesign for a hot key that keeps causing incidents across many jobs rather than patching each job one at a time.

keyPoints: Partition pruning: only read relevant partitions
Broadcast join: broadcast small table to all executors
Avoid shuffles: coalesce vs repartition, bucket joins
